passage: The canteen was roaring with lunch noise when Payal sat down next to Noor and said, "My dad's going to work in Dubai for a year." Noor almost said, "Wow, you'll get chocolates!" but she stopped. Payal's voice was flat, her shoulders were hunched, and she was tearing her roti into tiny pieces without eating. Noor leaned closer so she could hear over the clatter and just said, "A whole year?" Payal nodded and kept talking about the airport and her mum being quiet at home. Noor didn't interrupt once. When Payal finished, Noor pushed her own biscuits across.

qa.q: What was Payal doing with her roti?
qa.a: Tearing it into tiny pieces without eating.

qa.q: Why did Noor stop herself from saying "you'll get chocolates"?
qa.a: She noticed Payal's flat voice and hunched shoulders and guessed her friend was sad, not excited.

qa.q: How could Noor keep supporting Payal over the next few weeks?
qa.a: Check in now and then, keep listening without rushing to cheer her up, and let Payal lead what she wants to talk about.

qa.q: If you were Payal, what would Noor's quiet listening mean to you?
qa.a: It would feel like being taken seriously, which is often more comforting than advice or jokes. 🤍

grounding: It shows a girl reading a friend's posture and voice in a noisy canteen and listening without interrupting.

passage: On the steps of their building in Mumbai, Nikita was telling Rukmini about her dance audition. "And then the music stopped in the middle, and—" "Same thing happened to me once!" Rukmini cut in, and started her own story. Halfway through, she noticed Nikita had crossed her arms and was looking at the lift, not at her. Her mouth was a thin line. Rukmini stopped. "Sorry. I took over. What happened when the music stopped?" Nikita slowly uncrossed her arms. "I kept dancing without it." Rukmini said nothing, just waited. Nikita smiled a little and told the rest.

qa.q: Where were Nikita and Rukmini sitting?
qa.a: On the steps of their building in Mumbai.

qa.q: What did Rukmini think Nikita's crossed arms and thin mouth meant?
qa.a: She read them as signs that Nikita felt cut off and annoyed that her story had been taken over.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do after noticing, and why did it work?
qa.a: She apologised, asked about Nikita's story and then waited quietly, which showed she was really listening.

qa.q: How might Nikita have felt when Rukmini said "I took over"?
qa.a: Relieved and respected, since her friend noticed without being told.

grounding: It shows a girl noticing a friend's body language, stopping her interruptions and listening.

passage:
"How was school?" Sabina asked.
"Fine." Naveen dropped his bag and went straight to his room, shoes still on.
"Fine with your shoes still on?" She followed and sat on the floor by his bed. "You don't have to talk."
"...Nobody picked me for kabaddi."
Sabina opened her mouth, then closed it. She waited.
"They picked Bunty before me. Bunty!"
"Hmm."
"And then I sat alone by the tap." He rubbed his eyes quickly.
"That sounds rotten," Sabina said quietly. "Want to practise raids with me after tea?"
Naveen's shoulders dropped. "Maybe."

qa.q: Which game was Naveen not picked for?
qa.a: Kabaddi.

qa.q: How did Sabina seem to feel when Naveen said "Fine" and went straight to his room?
qa.a: She seemed concerned, because his going straight to his room with his shoes still on suggested something was wrong.

qa.q: Which of Sabina's choices helped Naveen open up?
qa.a: Saying he didn't have to talk and then waiting quietly gave him space, instead of pushing him with questions.

qa.q: What might Naveen feel when his shoulders drop?
qa.a: Some relief, because his sister listened without judging and offered something to do together.

grounding: It shows a sister decoding her brother's body cues and listening without interrupting until he shares.

passage: Last month my friend Vikas told me his grandfather was in hospital. I started saying, 'My Nani was in hospital too, and—' Then I saw his shoulders were hunched and he was picking at his thumbnail. He wasn't looking at me. So I stopped talking. I just said, 'Hmm,' and waited. He kept going. He told me he was scared the house would be quiet without Dadaji's radio. I nodded and didn't interrupt once. At the end he said, 'Thanks for listening, Nikita.' I think it helped more than my Nani story would have.

qa.q: Where was Vikas's grandfather?
qa.a: He was in hospital.

qa.q: What made Nikita stop telling the Nani story?
qa.a: Nikita noticed Vikas's hunched shoulders, nail-picking and averted eyes, and realised he needed to be heard, not to hear Nikita's story.

qa.q: Which listening move helped Vikas open up?
qa.a: Stopping, saying 'Hmm' and waiting without interrupting gave him space to share his real worry.

qa.q: How might Vikas have felt if Nikita had kept talking about Nikita's Nani?
qa.a: He might have felt unheard and kept his fear to himself. 🤍

grounding: Illustrates a child listening without interrupting and reading a friend's body language, told in first person.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Pradeep Sir, Class 6 peer circle
At the start of term, Vishal often cut in while others spoke and missed their cues. Today, during the talking-stick round, a quiet girl said her weekend was 'fine' while staring at the floor, arms folded. Vishal waited until she finished, then said gently, 'You don't look fine. Want to talk after?' She nodded. He didn't interrupt anyone for the whole session. I told him privately that I noticed his careful listening, and he grinned. 😊

qa.q: What did the quiet girl say about her weekend?
qa.a: She said it was 'fine' while staring at the floor, arms folded.

qa.q: What does Vishal's comment 'You don't look fine' suggest about his thinking?
qa.a: It suggests he noticed the mismatch between her words and her body posture, and cared enough to check gently.

qa.q: How could Pradeep Sir help other students build this skill?
qa.a: He could run small games on reading faces and posture, and praise waiting until someone finishes speaking.

qa.q: How might the quiet girl feel after Vishal's question?
qa.a: She may feel seen and cared for, since someone noticed she wasn't really fine.

grounding: Shows a child learning to listen without interrupting and to read non-verbal cues, in a counsellor's note.

passage:
Reena's diary, Monday
Raghav was quiet all day. At lunch he said he didn't care about losing the chess final, but his shoulders were up by his ears and he kept rubbing the same spot on the table. I nearly started telling him about my own match. Then I remembered what Ma says: close your mouth, open your ears. So I just sat. After a while he told me he'd practised every night for a month. I didn't interrupt once. He ate half my paratha afterwards, which I think means he felt better.

qa.q: What final did Raghav lose?
qa.a: The chess final.

qa.q: What did Raghav's raised shoulders and rubbing suggest to Reena?
qa.a: That he was more upset and disappointed than he admitted.

qa.q: What did Reena get right, and what could she try next?
qa.a: Reena listened without interrupting; next Reena could ask a gentle question about how he's feeling.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel after talking to Reena?
qa.a: Lighter and less alone, since someone listened properly.

grounding: Shows a child noticing a friend's body cues and listening without interrupting.

passage: At the village school, Gurleen was explaining her plan for the science fair: a solar cooker made from a box and foil. Yusuf, eleven, kept cutting in. "No, use a bucket. No, make it bigger." Gurleen stopped. She folded her arms and looked out of the window. Yusuf noticed the folded arms and the way her voice had gone flat. He shut his mouth. "Sorry. Tell me the rest." She looked at him, unfolded her arms, and explained. He waited till she finished before he asked anything.

qa.q: What was Gurleen planning to make?
qa.a: A solar cooker made from a box and foil.

qa.q: What did Gurleen's folded arms suggest?

qa.q: What did Yusuf do that helped?
qa.a: He noticed her body language, apologised and listened until she finished.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel after Yusuf changes?

grounding: Shows a child noticing a friend's body cues and changing to listen without interrupting.

passage: In a São Paulo school yard, Mina told Priscila about her new school. "It's fine," she said, smiling. Priscila, ten, noticed the smile didn't reach Mina's eyes, and that Mina kept pulling at her sleeve. Priscila didn't jump in with her own news. She waited. "Fine?" she asked gently. Mina looked down. "Nobody sits with me at lunch." Priscila listened to the whole story before saying, "Then I'll call you at lunch on Saturday, and we'll plan something."

qa.q: What did Mina keep pulling at?
qa.a: Her sleeve.

qa.q: What might Priscila have been thinking when she noticed Mina's smile?
qa.a: She was concerned that Mina was hiding sadness behind the word "fine".

qa.q: What could Priscila suggest next to help Mina?

qa.q: What is it like for Mina when Priscila asks "Fine?"
qa.a: She probably feels seen and relieved to tell the truth.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's non-verbal cues and listening fully before responding.

passage: In the school library, Damini sat hunched over a book she wasn't reading. Hemant slid into the chair beside her. "What happened?" "My dog ran off on Sunday. We looked everywhere." Hemant opened his mouth. He'd lost a kite on Sunday, and it had been terrible. But Damini's chin was tucked down and she kept twisting her pencil. He closed his mouth and waited. "Mummy made posters," she said. "Nobody's called." Hemant nodded, not saying anything, until she finished. Then he said, "Can I help put up more posters after school?" Damini looked up for the first time.

qa.q: When did Damini's dog run off?
qa.a: On Sunday.

qa.q: What did Damini's tucked chin and twisting pencil tell Hemant about how she felt?
qa.a: They suggested she felt sad and worried, so it wasn't the moment for his own story.

qa.q: Which of Hemant's choices helped Damini open up?
qa.a: He held back his own kite story, waited quietly until Damini finished, and then offered real help.

qa.q: What would change if Hemant had told his kite story first?
qa.a: Damini might have felt unheard and shut down instead of opening up.

grounding: In a school library, a boy holds back his own story and reads a friend's body language to listen fully.

passage: I'm Dolma. I sit behind Vaibhav in Class 5. On Tuesday the new girl, Rinzin, was telling us about her old school. She talked fast and her arms were crossed tight. Vaibhav didn't interrupt once, which surprised me, because he usually does. When she finished, he said, "You must miss them a lot." Rinzin's arms came down. I don't know how he knew; maybe it was the crossed arms or the way she didn't smile once. After that she sat with us at lunch. I've started watching people's arms now too.

qa.q: What was Rinzin telling them about?
qa.a: Her old school.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav have noticed that told him Rinzin was sad?
qa.a: He likely noticed her tightly crossed arms, fast talking and lack of smiles, and guessed she missed her old friends.

qa.q: What worked in how Vaibhav responded?
qa.a: He listened without interrupting and then named what she might be feeling, which helped her relax.

qa.q: How does Dolma see Vaibhav's listening?
qa.a: Dolma is surprised because Vaibhav usually interrupts, and is now inspired to watch for body cues too.

grounding: A classmate watches a boy listen without interrupting and read a new girl's crossed arms.

passage:
Devika, come here. You were interrupting your friend again on the phone. Let your Preeti Dadi tell you something.

When I was ten, my best friend Kamla came to my house and said her father's shop had burned down. I was so eager to help that I kept talking: "Don't worry, my father will help, we'll give you money..." She stopped talking.

My mother took me aside. "Look at her shoulders," she said. Kamla's were hunched, her eyes on the floor.

So I went back and just sat. I didn't say anything. After a while, Kamla told me everything, how scared she was.

That's when I learned, Devika: listening is not waiting to talk. It's watching too.

qa.q: What happened to Kamla's father's shop?
qa.a: Her father's shop had burned down.

qa.q: How did Kamla feel when young Preeti kept talking?
qa.a: Kamla felt overwhelmed and scared, which is why she stopped talking and hunched her shoulders.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help Kamla?
qa.a: Preeti's mother pointed out Kamla's body language, so Preeti sat quietly, which let Kamla share her fears.

qa.q: How might Preeti's mother have felt watching her daughter?
qa.a: Her mother was likely concerned and wanted to teach her kindly how to listen.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, at ten, she learned to listen without interrupting and to read a friend's body language.

passage:
The school bus was packed and noisy on the rainy afternoon, windows fogged, children shouting. Ojas, ten, sat next to Pankaj and spoke very quietly.

"My dog is at the vet."

Pankaj almost said, "Mine got sick once too!" but stopped. He saw that Ojas's hands were twisting his tie and his eyes were red.

So he leaned closer, didn't interrupt, and just nodded.

Ojas kept talking. "Mummy says he might need an operation."

Pankaj said, "That sounds scary." Ojas nodded and leaned against him for the rest of the ride.

qa.q: Where was Ojas's dog?
qa.a: His dog was at the vet.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj stop himself from talking about his own dog?
qa.a: Pankaj felt concerned when he saw Ojas twisting his tie with red eyes, and sensed Ojas was upset and needed to be heard.

qa.q: What did Pankaj do well as a listener?
qa.a: He stopped himself from talking about his own dog, noticed Ojas's cues, and let him finish.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel after Pankaj listened?
qa.a: Ojas likely felt comforted and supported, leaning against him.

grounding: On a noisy monsoon bus, a child listens without interrupting and reads his friend's non-verbal cues.

passage:
It was the last day before the Christmas holidays at the school in Delhi. Jeevan, eleven, sat on the stairs with his arms crossed, looking at his shoes.

Lalremsiami sat next to him. "You okay?"

"My puppy got lost yesterday."

She didn't say anything. She waited.

"We looked everywhere," Jeevan continued. "Papa put up posters."

Lalremsiami noticed his lip trembling. She didn't interrupt or tell him it would be fine. She just said, "That's really hard."

Jeevan uncrossed his arms. "Thanks for listening."

qa.q: What did Jeevan's Papa do?
qa.a: Papa put up posters.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami stay quiet instead of saying it would be fine?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt concerned, seeing Jeevan's crossed arms and trembling lip, and sensed he was sad and needed to be heard first.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami show active listening?
qa.a: She waited, didn't interrupt or rush to reassure, and named how hard it was.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel when he uncrossed his arms?
qa.a: Jeevan likely felt relieved and supported, more open after being heard.

grounding: Before the Christmas holidays, a child listens without interrupting and reads a friend's body language.

passage:
"Sudha, you're not playing Holi with us?" Saurabh asked. She stood by the school gate, arms folded, eyes on her shoes.
"I just don't feel like it."
Saurabh started, "Come on, it's fun, you'll..." then stopped. Her shoulders were up near her ears. He waited.
"My new kurta," she said finally. "Ma saved up for it. If it gets coloured..."
"Oh." He nodded. "So you do want to play, just not in that."
"Yes!"
"I've got an old T-shirt in my bag. It's huge on me."
Sudha looked up for the first time. "Really?"
"Really."

qa.q: What did Sudha not want to get coloured?
qa.a: Her new kurta.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh stop mid-sentence and wait?
qa.a: He noticed Sudha's raised shoulders and felt concerned that something was wrong, so he chose to listen instead of pushing.

qa.q: What could Saurabh try next time a friend goes quiet?
qa.a: He could do the same again: notice body cues, stop talking, and give the friend time to explain.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel when Saurabh offers his T-shirt?
